title: Dashboards, SLIs, SLOs and alerts
summary: Turn telemetry into targets: pick a few SLIs that reflect what users feel (availability, time to first output, tool reliability, runaway runs, cost, quality), set SLOs from your own baseline and page on error-budget burn rate instead of raw thresholds.
useIf: You must define what healthy means for an LLM or agent service, and when to wake someone up.
avoidIf: You copy someone else's numbers or alert on every dip in a noisy quality score.

explain.md: An **SLI** is a measured ratio of good events to all events. An **SLO** is the target for it over a window. Google's SRE Workbook gives the method: choose SLIs from user experience, set the SLO from your own baseline and use the **error budget** (1 minus the SLO) to decide when to alert [[r21]]. The suggestions below are design ideas, not vendor numbers.

explain.title: Burn rate
explain.expr: burn rate = observed error rate / (1 - SLO)

vars.v: Target ratio of good events, for example 0.999 over 30 days
1 - SLO, for example 0.1 percent of events

explain.example: With a 99.9 percent SLO over 30 days, a constant 0.1 percent error rate is a burn rate of 1 and spends exactly the budget. An error rate of 1.44 percent sustained for one hour is a burn rate of 14.4 and spends 2 percent of the 30-day budget (14.4 x 1 h / 720 h).

explain.caption: Starting alert policy from the SRE Workbook [[tr1]]
head: Window
Budget consumed
Burn rate
Action

explain.md: The Workbook recommends 2 percent in one hour and 5 percent in six hours as reasonable starting numbers for paging, and 10 percent in three days for tickets, and says the right values depend on the service. Use a short window of one twelfth of the long window to cut false alerts and speed recovery, and suppress duplicate pages when several rules fire together [[tr1]]. Alert on **metrics**, which are not sampled, and use traces to explain the alert [[r15]].

use: Define SLIs from user-visible outcomes and measure them from unsampled metrics
Use multi-window burn-rate alerts for paging and a slow-burn ticket alert
Exclude human approval waits from latency SLIs so slow people do not burn budget
avoid: Do not page on raw token counts or single slow requests
Do not set SLOs without a measured baseline
Do not treat an LLM-judge score from a tiny sample as a paging signal
flips: Traffic is low: widen windows or use ticket-level alerts, since a few failures can swing ratios
Quality is the product: promote a validated quality SLI, but keep it ticket-level until agreement with human review is established
Runs wait on humans: measure compute time and approval time as separate SLIs

pitfalls.symptom: Pages fire constantly during busy hours and nobody trusts them
pitfalls.cause: Static latency thresholds ignore load and prompt mix
pitfalls.fix: Move to SLO burn-rate alerts with a short and a long window [[tr1]]

pitfalls.symptom: Latency SLO burns every time a human approval is pending
pitfalls.cause: Approval waits are counted as service latency
pitfalls.fix: Exclude paused time from the latency SLI and track approval time separately

pitfalls.symptom: A quality alert flaps between pass and fail
pitfalls.cause: The score comes from a small sample or an uncalibrated LLM judge
pitfalls.fix: Increase sample size, calibrate against human labels and alert on a rolling pass rate

scenarios.title: A customer-facing streaming assistant
scenarios.situation: A chat assistant streams answers to customers all day. Users complain when the first words take too long or when answers are wrong, not when a request takes 20 seconds in total.
unknowns: What does the baseline p95 first-chunk time look like?
How is answer quality sampled and judged?
scenarios.question: Which SLIs and alerts do you set?

options.name: SLIs on availability and p95 time to first chunk with burn-rate paging, plus a sampled quality pass rate as a ticket alert
options.why: It measures what users feel, pages on fast budget burn and keeps the noisy quality signal at ticket level.
options.tradeoff: You maintain several SLOs and an online evaluation pipeline.

options.name: A single p95 total-duration threshold
options.why: Total duration scales with answer length and ignores first-token delay and quality.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a non-streaming batch endpoint.

options.name: Page on every quality score drop
options.tradeoff: Noisy and may wake people for judge variance.

flips.if: The judge is validated against human labels
flips.then: Promote the quality SLI to a paging signal.

scenarios.takeaway: Measure what users feel and page on budget burn.

scenarios.title: A nightly agent pipeline with a deadline
scenarios.situation: A batch of 5,000 agent tasks must finish by 06:00. Individual task latency is irrelevant. Failures should be retried automatically.
unknowns: How many failures can retries absorb?
How early must an on-call know?
scenarios.question: How do you define health and alerts?

options.name: SLI: share of tasks completed by the deadline, ticket alert on projected shortfall, page when the projection crosses a hard limit
options.why: It tracks the outcome the business cares about and gives time to react before the deadline.
options.tradeoff: Needs a projection of progress, not only counts.

options.name: Per-task p95 latency alerts
options.why: Latency of single tasks does not predict whether the batch meets its deadline.
options.tradeoff: Useful as a diagnostic after the deadline slips.

options.name: Alert only when the batch fails
options.tradeoff: Learns of a missed deadline too late.

flips.if: Tasks are retried and failures cluster
flips.then: Add per-tool error SLIs to find the cause.

scenarios.takeaway: Pick the SLI that matches the promise you made.

quiz.q: An SLO of 99.5 percent over 30 days is in force. In the last hour the error rate was 7.2 percent. What is the burn rate?
quiz.hint: Error budget is 1 minus the SLO.
quiz.explain: The error budget is 0.5 percent. Burn rate is observed error rate over budget: 7.2 / 0.5 = 14.4, the page-level rate for a one-hour window.

quiz.q: Why should a latency SLI for an approval-gated agent exclude time paused for human approval?
options: Approval time is always under one second
Approval waits reflect human response time, not service quality, and would burn the budget unfairly
SLIs must not include p95 values
quiz.explain: Human delays are not service latency. Approvals can be traced, they are often long and p95 is a normal SLI statistic.

quiz.q: Put the steps of setting an SLO-based alert in order.
items: Choose an SLI that reflects user experience
Measure a baseline from unsampled metrics
Set the SLO and compute the error budget
quiz.explain: The SLI comes first, the baseline grounds the SLO, the budget defines burn-rate thresholds and review closes the loop.

flashcards.back: Observed error rate divided by the error budget (1 minus the SLO). A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the budget over the window.

flashcards.front: What starting alert numbers does the SRE Workbook suggest?
flashcards.back: Page at 2 percent budget in 1 hour (burn rate 14.4) and 5 percent in 6 hours (burn rate 6). Ticket at 10 percent in 3 days (burn rate 1).

flashcards.front: Why alert on metrics and not traces?
flashcards.back: Metrics are not sampled, so rates are accurate. Traces explain an alert after it fires.
